sources.title: Human History Map civilization index
sources.note: Exact id, display name, culture kind, approximate 1500 to 500 BCE lifetime, and historical-basemaps provenance.

sources.title: Human History Map research coverage ledger
sources.note: Three observed intervals, three border files, no outside-lifetime features, and missing content status.

sources.title: Human History Map 2000 BCE borders
sources.note: Predecessor seam uses a separate Koreans id over a much larger peninsula-and-Manchuria polygon.

sources.title: Human History Map 1500 BCE borders
sources.note: First exact Paleo-Koreans polygon, its topology, bounds, points, exclusions, and neighbors.

sources.title: Human History Map 1000 BCE borders
sources.note: Unchanged exact polygon for the 1000 to 700 BCE interval and adjacent Western Zhou, Sinic, and Late Jomon layers.

sources.title: Human History Map 700 BCE borders
sources.note: Unchanged exact polygon for the 700 to 500 BCE interval and adjacent Eastern Zhou, Sinic, and Late Jomon layers.

sources.title: Human History Map 500 BCE borders
sources.note: The exact target vanishes at its indexed endpoint and audited Korean points have no mapped owner.

sources.title: Human History Map 400 BCE borders
sources.note: Later seam introduces Gojoseon across a differently shaped peninsula-and-Liaodong area.

sources.title: Bronze Age: Development of Farming, Villages, and Metals
sources.note: National Museum of Korea gallery guide to plain pottery, village farming, stone tools, rare bronze, ornaments, and dolmens.

sources.title: Gochang, Hwasun and Ganghwa Dolmen Sites
sources.note: UNESCO synthesis of hundreds of first-millennium BCE dolmens, quarrying, transport, tomb construction, and research value.

sources.title: Rice in ancient Korea: status symbol or community food?
sources.note: Archaeobotanical evidence from Sangdong-dong and Songguk-ri tests whether rice was restricted to elites.

sources.title: Millet vs rice: evaluating farming and language dispersal in Korea
sources.note: Open archaeological critique separates material change and crop movement from uncertain prehistoric language assignment.

sources.title: Agricultural origins in the Korean Peninsula
sources.note: Direct scientific evidence and archaeobotanical methods for early cultivation on the peninsula.

sources.title: Population Fluctuation and Adoption of Food Production in Prehistoric Korea
sources.note: Summed radiocarbon probabilities test population change around millet and rice adoption without assuming simple causation.

sources.title: Intragroup social differentiation and household inequality in Mumun settlements
sources.note: Gini analysis of house sizes and pottery across seventy-three settlements finds cooperation alongside household wealth differences.

sources.title: Paddy rice, aggregation, and Mumun social organization in Ulsan
sources.note: Settlement-distribution study connects paddy labor, aggregation, permanent villages, and social organization cautiously.

sources.title: Enhanced dietary reconstruction of Korean prehistoric populations
sources.note: Open compound-specific isotope study of people and animals from dated Mumun sites, with preservation and sampling cautions.

sources.title: Direct isotopic evidence for millet consumption in the Middle Mumun
sources.note: Human bone collagen demonstrates important foxtail and broomcorn millet consumption in central inland communities.

sources.title: Stable isotope evidence of human diet at Nukdo shell midden
sources.note: Human and animal isotope study tests terrestrial, marine, and plant foods near the late Mumun boundary.

sources.title: Population movements through the archaeology of textile production
sources.note: Open synthesis documents spindle whorls and weights at Early and Middle Mumun sites while keeping linguistic inference separate.

sources.title: Late Holocene climate variability in central Korea
sources.note: Pollen, geochemistry, and fire records reconstruct changing monsoon conditions and possible, not deterministic, social impacts.

sources.title: The Transition from Foraging to Farming in Prehistoric Korea
sources.note: Current Anthropology review uses archaeobotany to evaluate environment, mobility, migration, and mixed food strategies.

sources.title: Carbonized Crops from Songguk-ri and Plant Cultivation in the Mumun Period
sources.note: Flotation and wet-sieving recovered rice, wheat, two millets, soybean, and azuki bean from houses and pits.

sources.title: Buyeo Songguk-ri Prehistoric Settlement
sources.note: Academy of Korean Studies site report covers twenty-five excavation seasons, 117 houses, pits, fences, buildings, graves, crops, and tools.

sources.title: Archaeological Site in Songguk-ri, Buyeo
sources.note: Korea Heritage Service record establishes protected-site identity and official archaeological status.

sources.title: Prehistorical Gangwon permanent exhibition
sources.note: National museum evidence for harvesting knives, preserved willow arrow shafts, daggers, mirrors, and regional Bronze Age craft.

sources.title: The Dolmen Garden
sources.note: Chuncheon National Museum records excavated and restored local dolmens with pottery and harvesting tools.

sources.title: Semi-lunar Stone Knife
sources.note: National Museum description explains shapes, hand loops, and use for harvesting grain ears.

sources.title: Liaoning-type Bronze Dagger
sources.note: Museum object history dates the dagger tradition and explains detachable hilts and Liaoning connections.

sources.title: Mirrors with Fine Linear Designs
sources.note: Museum conservation account explains alloying, sand casting, polishing, burial contexts, and ritual interpretations near the later boundary.

sources.title: Landscapes shared by visibility in Songguk-ri culture
sources.note: Spatial analysis of foothill settlements, water and farmland access, storage, craft, visibility, and possible kin connections.

sources.title: Archaeology of Early Agriculture in the Korean Peninsula
sources.note: Open research review describes fields, settlements, river settings, ditches, dating, and regional agricultural variability.

sources.title: Paleoparasitology of historical toilets and mummies in South Korea
sources.note: Review explicitly finds no conclusively identified Bronze Age toilet and distinguishes evidence from later facilities.

sources.title: Physical Anthropology of Bronze Age People on the Korean Peninsula
sources.note: Review of the small, uneven excavated skeletal sample and limits on biological or ethnic conclusions.

sources.title: A History of the Korean Language
sources.note: Cambridge history explains late written evidence, later Three Kingdoms transcriptions, and limits of Old Korean reconstruction.

sources.title: Archaeolinguistic evidence for Koreanic dispersal
sources.note: Study emphasizes that archaeological materials can move without securely identifying spoken language and records are late.

sources.title: Idu writing
sources.note: Academy of Korean Studies account dates surviving Korean-language Chinese-character adaptations to the Three Kingdoms and later eras.

sources.title: Discontinuous spread of millet agriculture in eastern Asia
sources.note: Open multi-region study tracks dated millet movement without equating crops, genes, languages, or ethnic groups.

sources.title: Wild resources and resilience in early East Asian agriculture
sources.note: Large archaeobotanical compilation shows changing but continuing use of nuts and wild plants alongside crops.

sources.title: Social Change and Household Geography in Mumun South Korea
sources.note: Household archaeology traces spatial segmentation and a shift toward smaller dwellings without naming exact family systems.

sources.title: Women and Femininity in Prehistoric Korea
sources.note: Gender archaeology review warns that sparse evidence and older research practices often make women archaeologically invisible.

sources.title: Leadership in the Emergent Baekje State
sources.note: Later state-formation study reviews Mumun palisades, ditches, burned houses, daggers, and arrowheads as possible conflict evidence.

sources.title: How are Bronze Objects Made?
sources.note: National Museum notes rare bronze, uncertain local copper smelting, absent peninsula tin deposits, and casting evidence.

sources.title: Production and distribution of red-burnished pottery in the Nam River basin
sources.note: Metric analysis distinguishes largely household plain pottery from wider-circulating, more specialized red-burnished wares.

sources.title: Geochemical pXRF analysis of Korean Bronze Age pottery
sources.note: Non-destructive portable X-ray fluorescence study tests ceramic composition and provenance rather than relying only on appearance.

sources.title: Bronze Culture of Korea
sources.note: National Museum journal distinguishes regional bronze traditions, dates, stone-tool coexistence, and contested ethnic interpretations.

sources.title: The Pyeonggeo-dong settlements
sources.note: Large salvage project combines AMS dating, field soils, crop remains, footprints, and settlement sequences.

sources.title: Bronze Age settlement nucleation in the North Han River basin
sources.note: Radiocarbon and bootstrap study cautions against treating pottery types as exact population clocks at Jungdo.

sources.title: Attached-rim pottery in Seoul and Gyeonggi
sources.note: National Museum journal uses associations and typology to track later pottery change near and beyond the card endpoint.

proposedOverrides.summary: An evidence-aware guide to localized Mumun-period communities inside the atlas’s anachronistically named Paleo-Koreans polygon, with exact geometry, daily life, research methods and later-language guardrails.
